arxiv:2611.18490.title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
arxiv:2611.18490.abstract: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

doi:10.1002/ange.9097834.title: Coking–Crosslinking Competition Shapes Alveolar Hard Carbon Formation From Heterogeneous Precursors for Wide‐Temperature Sodium Storage
doi:10.1002/ange.9097834.abstract: Competing with lithium‐ion technology on cost and resource abundance requires sodium‐ion batteries to use hard‐carbon anodes produced from abundant, inexpensive feedstocks without sacrificing structural control. Yet the natural and residual feedstocks that meet these requirements are typically chemically heterogeneous. Competing transformations among their constituent fractions before high‐temperature treatment make the carbonization pathway and carbon architecture difficult to predict and direct. Here, controlled fraction removal and reintroduction reveal a new mechanism whereby coking‐crosslinking competition selects the carbonization pathway. Surface coking blocks oxygen access and suppresses bulk crosslinking, whereas low‐temperature pre‐purification removes coking‐prone fractions, preserving an oxygen‐accessible skeleton that forms alveolar hard carbon (AHC). Operando x‐ray diffraction (XRD)/Raman and synchrotron x‐ray absorption near‐edge structure (XANES) establish that the low‐potential plateau arises from reversible formation of highly reduced sodium species within confined pores. AHC‐120@15‐1400 delivers 388.3 mAh g −1 with 91.3% initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), retains 94.3% capacity after 10 500 cycles at 4 A g −1 , and operates from −25°C to 45°C. A 1.2 Ah pouch cell retains 82.5% capacity after 1,000 cycles, while the route lowers cradle‐to‐gate material‐resource impact by 35.6% relative to commercial hard‐carbon production. Controlling coking‐crosslinking competition establishes a pathway‐selective design principle for converting heterogeneous carbon resources into durable, wide‐temperature sodium‐storage carbons.

doi:10.1039/d6ra09929g.abstract: This work highlights current developments in pure, porous, and heteroatom-doped graphene as anode materials for SIBs. Additionally, it addresses graphene nanocomposite anodes, particularly conversion, intercalation, and alloy-based materials.

doi:10.53941/sen.2026.100015.title: Highly Stable and Practical Sodium-Ion Batteries: Key Materials, Electrode Engineering, Manufacturing, and Prospects
doi:10.53941/sen.2026.100015.abstract: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are promising for large-scale energy storage owing to abundant sodium resources, low cost, and good manufacturing compatibility. However, their practical application remains limited by the structural stability of key materials, interfacial side reactions, cycle life, and safety. This review focuses on highly stable and practical SIBs and systematically summarizes the main failure mechanisms and stabilization strategies of cathode materials, anode materials, and electrolyte/electrode interfaces. Particular attention is paid to phase-transition suppression in layered oxides, framework strengthening of polyanionic compounds, defect regulation in Prussian blue/white materials, closed-pore structure optimization of hard carbon, solid electrolyte interphase (SEI)/cathode electrolyte interphase (CEI) formation, and interfacial stability of solid-state electrolytes. In addition, engineering strategies such as thick-electrode design, dry electrode manufacturing, thermal management, adaptive binders, and digital twin technologies are discussed from the perspective of material–electrode–device integration. Distinct from reviews centered on individual material classes, this work connects key-material failure mechanisms with electrode architecture, manufacturing, safety management, and industrialization, providing a full-chain materials–electrode–device–manufacturing perspective. Future efforts should focus on interfacial controllability, manufacturing consistency, and recycling sustainability to accelerate the large-scale application of SIBs.

doi:10.1021/acsami.6c19377.title: Molecular Engineering of Customizable Resin-Derived Hard Carbon Framework for Efficient Sodium Storage
doi:10.1021/acsami.6c19377.abstract: Owing to their high carbon yield and molecular controllability, resins have emerged as promising precursors for hard carbon (HC) anodes in sodium-ion batteries (SIBs). However, achieving synergistic optimization of carbon microcrystals and sub-nanopores during resin pyrolysis to enhance sodium storage capacity remains a significant challenge. Herein, a spatial-chemistry-directed crosslinking (SCDC) strategy, based on the Mannich reaction of selected target molecules (TMs) within a resin network, is proposed. Owing to the steric hindrance of gem-dimethyl groups and the carboxyl-group-mediated interactions, the formation of nanoscale closed pores was facilitated while the continuity of sp2-hybridized carbon microcrystals was ensured and a large interlayer spacing was maintained. Through this approach, an HC architecture with elongated pseudo-graphitic domains and abundant closed pores is constructed in a synergistic manner, affording excellent electronic and ionic transport kinetics. The engineered HC exhibits an enhanced reversible capacity of 427.5 mAh g–1 and an outstanding initial coulombic efficiency (ICE) of 90.18%, along with a high reversible initial capacity of 346.7 mAh g–1 at 2 A g–1 and a capacity retention of up to 85.3% after 500 cycles. This study provides new insights into the microstructural design for high-capacity, high-rate sodium storage.

doi:10.1149/1945-7111/aec2ae.title: Effect of Cycling Protocol on the Stress and Mechanical Degradation of Hard Carbon Electrodes
doi:10.1149/1945-7111/aec2ae.abstract: Maximum stress experienced by an electrode during cycling is shown to cause mechanical degradation and capacity fade, but the effect of potential window and stress range (Δσ) on cycling behavior was not investigated. Here, stresses generated in hard carbon (HC)-based porous composite electrodes were measured in situ while cycling under three different potential windows: (i) full window (2-0.0005 V vs Na/Na+), (ii) sloping (2-0.1 V vs Na/Na+), and plateau (0.1-0.0005 V vs Na/Na+) regions and three different C-rates. The stress range (Δσ), capacity, and mechanical hysteresis during sloping region were nearly rate-independent, while they showed significant rate dependence in the plateau region, suggesting two different ion-storage mechanisms. Both the stress range and mechanical hysteresis (indicator of irreversible deformation) increased at lower current densities during the plateau region, indicating higher irreversible mechanical work and degradation. During extended cycling, capacity continued to decrease even after the maximum stress saturated, indicating that Δσ and hysteresis are important to explain electrode degradation. Based on these observations, an optimized cycling protocol was used which reduced stress range and mechanical hysteresis while increasing specific capacity at faster rate, demonstrating the importance of coupled electro-chemomechanical responses for optimizing cycling protocols to improve capacity utilization and mechanical durability.

doi:10.3390/batteries12110491.title: Waste-PET-Derived Nitrogen-Doped Hard Carbon for Sodium-Ion Batteries: A Comparative Study
doi:10.3390/batteries12110491.abstract: Sodium-ion batteries (SIBs) are regarded as a promising alternative to lithium-ion batteries (LIBs). However, their advancement is constrained by the sluggish kinetics and modest capacity of conventional hard carbon (HC) anodes. Here, we report an upcycling strategy that transforms post-consumer polyethylene terephthalate (PET) bottles into nitrogen-doped hard carbon (NHC) through KOH-assisted pyrolysis followed by a separate urea-assisted nitrogen-doping treatment. The resulting NHC exhibits enlarged interlayer spacing and incorporates nitrogen into the carbon structure. Benefiting from this tailored architecture, the optimized NHC-800 delivers a high reversible capacity of 310.7 mAh g−1 at 20 mA g−1 over 874 cycles. Furthermore, a comparative mechanistic investigation of HC, NHC, reduced graphene oxide (rGO), and carboxyl-functionalized multi-walled carbon nanotubes (MWCNTs-COOH) reveals architecture-dependent sodium-storage pathways, ranging from intersheet diffusion in rGO and kinetically asymmetric storage in oxidized nanotubes to adsorption–intercalation–nanopore filling in hard carbons. This study not only elucidates the principles of rational defect and spacing engineering for developing high-performance SIB anodes but also demonstrates a strategy to upcycle plastic waste, thereby reducing the landfill burden and mitigating dependence on critical lithium resources.

doi:10.3390/ma19224842.title: Biomass-Derived Hard Carbon Anodes for Sodium-Ion Batteries: From Precursor Chemistry to Multiscale Structural Engineering
doi:10.3390/ma19224842.abstract: Biomass-derived hard carbon (BHC) is a promising anode material for sodium-ion batteries owing to its renewable feedstocks, low cost, and favorable sodium-storage performance. However, variations in biomass composition and pyrolysis behavior pose challenges to precise structural regulation, thereby constraining further improvements in initial Coulombic efficiency (ICE), plateau capacity, and rate capability. This review analyzes how the decomposition and reconstruction of cellulose, hemicellulose, and lignin influence microcrystal, defect, and pore formation. In particular, this review discusses multiscale regulation strategies, including pretreatment to optimize precursor composition and interactions among constituents; pre-carbonization, pre-oxidation, and Joule heating to stabilize carbon frameworks and regulate carbon-layer growth and pore evolution; and surface engineering to reduce irreversible sodium consumption and improve interfacial stability. Finally, future perspectives, including establishing quantitative relationships between precursor characteristics and carbon structures, developing energy-efficient processes for coordinated structural regulation, and ensuring structural consistency across feedstock batches, are proposed. We believe this review can help guide the design of BHC for practical applications.

doi:10.1021/acsami.6c17291.title: Understanding the Role of Solid Polymer Electrolyte Network Structure and Modulus in In Situ Anode Formation of “Anode-Free” Sodium Metal Batteries
doi:10.1021/acsami.6c17291.abstract: “Anode-free” solid-state battery concepts based on sodium metal have attracted greater research interest recently due to their potential economic advantages, namely lower material costs and simplified, less expensive processing. However, these cell concepts suffer from poor cycling reversibility and cycle life, and little is understood about the fundamentals that govern sodium metal growth during in situ anode formation in solid-state batteries (SSBs). In this work, we use two model cross-linked network solid polymer electrolyte systems with varying cross-link density and modulus to investigate how such properties influence sodium metal growth and cycling stability. Using scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy, we show that solid polymer electrolyte (SPE) modulus strongly influences the early-stage morphology and charge-transfer kinetics of in situ formed sodium metal anodes. The higher-modulus SPE promotes faster in-plane growth of sodium metal, particularly during the early stages of in situ anode formation. Consequently, the higher-modulus SPE displays 3.0× and 1.9× lower interfacial resistances than the lower-modulus SPE at plating capacities of 0.05 and 0.1 mAh cm–2, respectively. Despite lower interfacial resistance early in anode formation, the higher-modulus SPE displays shorter cycle life in Na|SPE|Cu “anode-free” half cells at 2.3 ± 1.1 mAh cm–2 compared to 6.6 ± 2.9 for the lower-modulus SPE. This work demonstrates that tuning SPE network structure through cross-link density can increase modulus and accelerate electroactive Na-SPE interface formation, but improved interfacial kinetics do not necessarily translate to greater long-term cycling stability. In situ indentation experiments in SEM showed that increasing cross-link density also yields a more brittle network that is more susceptible to crack propagation, which likely facilitates dendrite penetration and reduces cycle life.

doi:10.1021/acsaem.6c02883.title: Mechanistic Insights into Sodium Storage through Transport Kinetics, Bulk, and Interfacial Property Analyses of Hard and Soft Carbon Anodes
doi:10.1021/acsaem.6c02883.abstract: Understanding the sodium storage mechanism in disordered carbons remains critical for the development of high-capacity anodes for sodium–ion batteries. Here, we systematically investigate sodium storage in hard carbon, soft carbon, and a hard–soft carbon composite by correlating carbon structure, ion transport kinetics, and electrochemical interfacial chemistry with electrochemical performance. The three carbon architectures exhibit distinct pore structures, surface chemistry, and graphitic ordering, enabling the contribution of surface/interfacial and pore-confined sodium storage to be differentiated. Kinetic analysis demonstrates that the sodium ion transport is strongly dependent on the accessible pore network and carbon microstructure. The hard–soft carbon showed the highest galvanostatic intermittent titration technique (GITT)-derived diffusion coefficients above 0.6 V but the steepest decrease below 0.1 V. Despite differences in the surface chemistries of the carbon materials, the interfacial chemistry remained similar, as did the initial coulombic efficiency and cycling stability. The increase in discharge capacity previously reported for the hard–soft carbon is therefore attributed mainly to the availability and connectivity of suitable nanopores. The findings provide mechanistic insights into the interplay between ion transport, carbon pore structure and accessibility, and interfacial chemistry, and explain why cocarbonization of a hard and soft carbon is a facile route for increasing capacity via pore structure modification, suggesting that restricted access to retained ultramicropores increases the low-voltage plateau capacity, while the oxygen-rich surface of the composite supports storage in the sloping region.

arxiv:2611.19116.title: A Hybrid State Space-Attention Architecture for Forecasting the Trajectories of Battery Degradation
arxiv:2611.19116.abstract: Early-life battery degradation trajectory forecasting aims to predict a battery cell's full state-of-health (SOH) trajectory from its initial charge-discharge cycles, potentially reducing cell qualification and evaluation time from months to days. Despite recent advances, accurate forecasting remains challenging for emerging battery chemistries, data-scarce domains, and cells exhibiting degradation behaviors beyond those observed during training. Existing state-of-the-art approaches increasingly rely on model scaling, large language model-derived aging-condition embeddings, and extensive fold-specific hyperparameter tuning, raising concerns about computational efficiency, reproducibility, and generalization. This work introduces DecayFormer, a compact hybrid state-space and attention architecture designed for early-life degradation trajectory forecasting. DecayFormer combines cycle-level selective recurrence, using a single scalar state per channel, with an attention mechanism queried by the recurrent state. It further incorporates state-of-charge (SOC) interval statistics and a master curve head that jointly estimates a scalar lifetime and a monotonically non-increasing SOH profile parameterized by normalized lifetime. We evaluate DecayFormer on the BatteryLife benchmark using all 22 aging-condition-exclusive folds, with a single run per fold and one fixed configuration across all folds, without fold-specific tuning. DecayFormer achieves mean test MAPE values of 2.25% on Li-ion, 2.76% on CALB, 0.95% on Na-ion, and 7.19% on Zn-ion. These results demonstrate the potential of compact sequence models to deliver accurate early-life degradation forecasts across diverse battery chemistries and aging conditions, without relying on extensive model scaling or per-fold optimization.

doi:10.1021/acsenergylett.6c02924.title: From Nonstep to Step: Voltage‑Response‑Driven Interfacial Evolution and Closed‑Pore Sodium Filling in Hard Carbon Anode
doi:10.1021/acsenergylett.6c02924.abstract: Hard carbon (HC) is regarded as the most commercially viable anode for sodium-ion batteries. However, during the initial discharge of the HC anode, the thick solid electrolyte interphase (SEI) derived from the decomposition of the ester-based electrolytes severely restricts sodium storage kinetics. Herein, we propose a customized discharge strategy that triggers a step voltage response (SR) in the HC anode to achieve rapid interfacial passivation. Through multiscale characterizations and theoretical calculations, we elucidate the underlying mechanism: the field-induced concentration effect within the interfacial electrolyte steers the decomposition pathways toward inorganic products, favoring the formation of a thin, uniform, and highly ionically conductive SEI. The accelerated interfacial kinetics significantly lowers the diffusion barrier, thereby enhancing the accessibility of closed pores for quasi-metallic sodium cluster storage. Consequently, the SR-treated HC anode delivers improved rate performance in both the sodium-ion full battery and hybrid capacitor. This study offers critical insights into the design of the formation protocol and provides a facile field-modulated strategy to enhance the sodium storage kinetics of the HC anode.

arxiv:2611.20749.title: Kinetic and Thermodynamic Limits of Sodium Pore Filling in Hard Carbon
arxiv:2611.20749.abstract: The low-voltage plateau-like capacity of hard carbon anodes is widely regarded as a key signature of sodium storage in closed pores, often defining the performance of Na-ion batteries. Here, we combine first-principles calculations with a grand canonical Monte Carlo pore-filling model to show that Na storage in closed pores is not governed by a single equilibrium-plateau mechanism but by a distribution of pore-specific thermodynamic and kinetic activation processes. Thermodynamically, the voltage at which Na pore filling becomes favorable decreases with increasing pore size. Kinetically, pore filling involves Na nucleation, coalescence, growth, and bulk diffusion. While small pores fill rapidly, large pores exhibit both a smaller thermodynamic stimulus and significant kinetic limitations. Nucleation can be accelerated by introducing defects at the pore walls, although an excessively high defect concentration slows bulk diffusion. This work shows that not all closed pores contribute equally to Na storage: some may be thermodynamically favorable but kinetically inactive under realistic charge/discharge rates. Because of this, the inverse design of hard carbon electrodes should target a kinetically accessible pore-size and defect-density window that balances high plateau-like capacity with fast-charging performance.
